title: Frequent MinIO SIGILL and SIGSEGV crashes initially attributed to gogo/protobuf
body: I am using MinIO RELEASE.2024-03-26T22-10-45Z (go1.21.8 linux/amd64). MinIO depends on the deprecated and unmaintained gogo/protobuf library, and I would prefer a supported alternative so future CVEs can be addressed. I discovered the dependency while investigating a segmentation violation on an older January 2024 deployment. The trace reports SIGILL, an unexpected return PC in github.com/gogo/protobuf/proto.extensionProperties, and MinIO internal/grid frames. We must update before filing a separate bug report about that crash.

symptoms_visible: My MinIO process terminates with SIGILL and an 'unexpected return pc' trace that includes github.com/gogo/protobuf/proto.extensionProperties and MinIO internal/grid frames.
N0.label: N0 protobuf concern and crash trace reported

symptoms_visible: The affected node repeatedly exits with both SIGILL and SIGSEGV at different addresses, sometimes restarting about every fifteen minutes.
Only one node has these crashes; the other seven nodes in the same cluster do not.
N1.label: N1 failure scope and platform established

symptoms_visible: MinIO still terminates with the same SIGILL error while running with GODEBUG=gcshrinkstackoff=1.
N2_x.label: N2_x stack-shrinking workaround aftermath

symptoms_visible: Without a memory limit, memory growth caused Linux OOM to kill other processes and crash the server; adding GOMEMLIMIT=128GiB made operation more predictable but did not remove the segmentation violations.
N3_x.label: N3_x garbage-collection workaround aftermath

symptoms_visible: The same SIGILL and SIGSEGV crashes remain after reinstalling the affected server while leaving its MinIO data untouched.
N4_x.label: N4_x operating-system remaster aftermath

symptoms_visible: The affected server continues to crash, while the seven otherwise identical cluster nodes remain stable.
N5.label: N5 server-specific platform difference found

symptoms_visible: After changing the affected server's HPE workload profile from 'Virtualization - Power Efficient' to 'HPC', MinIO no longer experiences the SIGILL and SIGSEGV crashes.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

question_patterns: Are all crashes showing the same stack, or do you also get other signals and program counters?
Can you share a summary of the recurring crash messages?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I get many instances of both SIGILL and SIGSEGV. The SIGSEGV messages use different addresses and PCs, including code=0x1 and code=0x2, rather than always failing in the same function.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every failure is the same deterministic panic from proto.extensionProperties with an ordinary Go error and no SIGILL or varied program counters.
The failures occur less frequently, but I still see the same mixture of SIGILL and SIGSEGV at varied addresses.

question_patterns: Does this happen on every node in the cluster or only on a particular machine?
Are otherwise equivalent nodes affected too?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Only this one node has the problem. The seven other nodes in the cluster do not have it at all, even though the servers are supposed to be identical.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: All eight nodes began crashing in the same way immediately after deploying the same MinIO binary.

question_patterns: How often does the affected MinIO process restart?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On this node MinIO is restarting about every fifteen minutes.

question_patterns: What architecture, processor, operating system and virtualization environment does the affected node use?
Please share the relevant CPU and platform details, including whether this is bare metal.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It is an amd64 bare-metal server with no virtualization layer, running Ubuntu 22.04 on an AMD EPYC 7702P 64-Core Processor. The CPU reports family 23, model 49, stepping 0 and microcode 0x830107a.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It is a virtual machine, and only VMs migrated to one hypervisor host show the illegal instructions.

question_patterns: Is MinIO compression enabled on this cluster?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Compression is off in this cluster.

edges.comment: The reporter later supplied repeated crash logs, the one-node-only scope, restart frequency and detailed bare-metal AMD platform information. These observations weaken attribution to a deterministic protobuf call-site defect.

solution.intent: Treat the trace as Go runtime stack corruption and disable stack shrinking with GODEBUG=gcshrinkstackoff=1.
solution.concrete_example: Run MinIO with GODEBUG=gcshrinkstackoff=1 and observe whether the SIGILL and SIGSEGV failures stop.
solution.inference_hint: The maintainer inferred from the impossible return PC and varied fatal signals that the named gogo/protobuf frame was where corrupted execution surfaced, not evidence that protobuf caused the corruption. The specific stack-shrinking workaround was nevertheless falsified by the reporter's test.

edges.comment: Actual failed attempt: the reporter ran with GODEBUG=gcshrinkstackoff=1 and still received the same SIGILL.

solution.intent: Disable Go garbage collection as a containment workaround, optionally adding a memory limit to make restarts more predictable.
solution.concrete_example: Start MinIO with GOGC=off; if unbounded growth is unsafe, combine it with GOMEMLIMIT=128GiB while investigating.

edges.comment: Actual failed and hazardous workaround: SIGSEGV persisted with GOGC=off, while an unbounded run caused Linux OOM to kill other processes. GOMEMLIMIT improved predictability but did not fix the crashes.

solution.intent: Reinstall the affected server's operating system while preserving its MinIO data, to eliminate node-local OS corruption or configuration drift.
solution.concrete_example: Re-master the affected node without touching its MinIO data, then observe whether the fatal signals recur.

edges.comment: Actual failed attempt: re-mastering the one affected server while preserving MinIO data had no effect.

question_patterns: Since reinstalling the OS did not help, what low-level machine configuration differs between this node and the seven healthy peers?
Can you compare the affected server with a healthy peer below the operating-system level and report any difference?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I found that the HPE workload profile on this server is set to 'Virtualization - Power Efficient'. The other servers use 'HPC'.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The affected server and every healthy peer have identical low-level platform settings; the only difference is the MinIO binary on this node.
The same profile mismatch is present, but the menu wording differs slightly on this server's firmware revision.
The affected chassis has a different asset-tag label.

edges.comment: The reporter independently compared the servers and found the decisive platform-level difference after application, GC and operating-system directions failed.

solution.intent: Correct the affected server's HPE workload profile to match the stable peers, then verify that MinIO no longer produces SIGILL or SIGSEGV.
solution.concrete_example: Change the affected HPE server's workload profile from 'Virtualization - Power Efficient' to 'HPC', as configured on the other seven servers, and monitor MinIO to confirm the fatal signals stop. The reporter suspected the profile may affect CPU scaling, but did not establish the exact setting-level mechanism.

edges.comment: Final accepted resolution: changing the server's HPE workload profile to HPC, matching the other nodes, stopped the crashes. CPU-governor effects were only the reporter's unverified speculation and are not scored as the precise mechanism.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause as the affected server's mismatched HPE workload profile: it used 'Virtualization - Power Efficient' while the stable peers used 'HPC'.
Must ground the diagnosis in the one-node-only scope, varied SIGILL/SIGSEGV failures, failed GC-related workarounds, unsuccessful operating-system remaster, and the platform-profile difference.
Must not attribute the crashes to gogo/protobuf merely because its function appears in a corrupted stack trace.
Must not present GODEBUG=gcshrinkstackoff=1, GOGC=off, or remastering the server as the fix; each was tried without resolving the crashes, and disabling GC also created an OOM risk.
Must recommend matching the affected server's profile to HPC and have the reporter verify that SIGILL and SIGSEGV stop before declaring resolution.
Must not claim that a particular CPU scaling-governor mechanism was proven; the reporter only suggested it as a possibility.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced production infrastructure operator who can manage an eight-node MinIO cluster, change Go runtime environment variables, inspect Linux and CPU details, collect scheduler traces, remaster a server, and compare firmware settings, but is not familiar with Go runtime internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, evidence-driven and detailed; challenges premature closure, supplies extensive logs and platform data, clearly reports failed workarounds, and follows up with the independently discovered resolution.
